quoted_text:
Exciting to see @GrailCo gaining momentum.

Been following since the beginning. It’s refreshing to see @1confirmation take a venture studio approach and execute in house, especially with all the current discourse around why crypto VCs stopped pursuing unique ideas.

It’s time to stop gatekeeping it :) 

I want to write a deeper piece, but for now a few observations:

1. Collector insight/edge comes from true passion! 

Grail is tokenizing trading cards, mostly sports.

The market for tokenized cards and digital packs is already crowded, but collectibles are not just a distribution problem. Value is driven by passion, taste, and collector pulse and platforms should act like good curators. 

You need to know what people actually care about before the market fully prices it.

A good example is gWemby, the fractional token for Wemby cards.

Wemby is one of the hottest players in the NBA right now. The 1confirmation team had the insight and right timing to acquire Wemby cards and list the asset around 20 days ago.

Since then, the physical Wemby card market has moved up  20- 30% and gWemby is backed by 50 of them. 

2. Fractionalized cards are the killer feature

- The EV on Grail packs is the highest I’ve seen in the market.

I’ve personally ripped a few dozen packs and saw 20 to 50% markups.

The fractional element is what makes this interesting. You can scale digital packs faster, with lower stock turnover, while market activity around the fractions helps to fund higher EV. 

That is very different from my experience on other platforms, where you spend a few hundred dollars and end up down 20 to 30%.

- Better price discovery for blue chip cards

Fractionalized cards make even more sense for high end blue chips.

Cards that trade for hundreds of thousands or millions are usually extremely scarce, which means fewer market signals. But a lot of people still want exposure.

@altxyzofficial, Grail’s vaulting partner, recently acquired a Kobe card for $3.15M.

That is exactly the type of asset that can only have real 24/7 live pricing through onchain fractionals.

$gMJ feels closer to that endgame. I also think limited drops, rare photo matched can benefit from it even on non huge valuation. 

3. Collectibles x PM angle

With Wemby, and sports cards more generally, real world events and cultural relevance directly impact the market.

Player performance, playoff moments, injuries, narratives, nostalgia, taste. All of it matters.

Anchoring onchain assets to external reality is one of the most exciting parts here(Different from pure RWA approach where price discovery is mostly taking place off chain) 

Grail recently gamified this by offering to double gWemby for holders if the Spurs won the game.

Collectibles are a phenomenal vehicle for this kind of prediction market hybrid. They already behaves like prediction markets with fandom attached.

Would recommend paying close attention.

the LLM's we know & love answer by writing an essay word by word - this is cool for complex tasks, but it results in slow & expensive outputs

this means 3 things, it technically can't "hallucinate" since it can't make things up, it's super fast & extremely cheap

it's best for huge systems that require a ton of classification & decision making based on inputs

A major $ZRO unlock is coming later today (UTC).

Around 23–26M $ZRO is scheduled to unlock, depending on the tracker - roughly 4.2% of released supply or ~6.7% of float on DefiLlama.

I’ve been tracking the large CEX movements around it, and so far the picture is more nuanced than “exchanges are preparing to dump.”

The Coinbase flows, for example, look consistent with hot–cold wallet rebalancing. One sequence moved 5.13M $ZRO through Prime Hot, with 3.38M later moved to cold custody. Similar patterns showed up across other venues.

There’s another important piece of context: as of May 31, LayerZero reported that 63.8% of investor-unlocked $ZRO was still held, while public-market sales averaged around 4.9M $ZRO per month.

So the headline unlock is not the same thing as immediate market supply.

On the demand side, @StargateFinance revenue already funds $ZRO buybacks, while the @LayerZero_Core protocol fee switch remains inactive. Zero + ATLAS are the future part of the value-capture thesis, not something absorbing this tranche today.

Supply is coming. The test is how much actually hits the market - and what bid is waiting for it.

text:
Claude Code fires 30 events per session

you can hang your own code on any of them

the 6 that changed how I work:

A hook is a shell command that runs at a fixed moment. It isn't a prompt

that's the whole point. The model can reason its way around an instruction. It can't reason its way around a hook

1. PreToolUse → before a tool runs, and it can block it

mine refuses any write to .env, and any rm it didn't explain first

2. PostToolUse → after a tool succeeds

mine runs the formatter on whatever file it just touched. I stopped asking for tidy code

3. UserPromptSubmit → after I hit enter, before the model sees it

mine attaches the branch and the last commit. every prompt. I never type it

4. Stop → the turn is finished

mine runs the tests. If they fail, the turn isn't finished

5. SessionStart → a session begins or resumes

mine prints the three things I changed yesterday and always forget

6. PreCompact → the moment before it compacts

mine saves the transcript. I've lost one. Not twice

they all live in .claude/settings.json. A matcher decides which tools they fire on

the other 24 are real (SubagentStop, FileChanged, PermissionDenied, WorktreeCreate). I've never needed one

start with PostToolUse. it's the one you feel today

Bookmark this. This is the one.

quoted_text:
The dead cat continues to bounce.  

What is Bitcoin, 17 years later? 

It’s not great for transactions or smart contracts; the user experience is still intimidating for most, and it’s no longer capturing the public’s imagination. 

If it comes up at the dinner party, it's followed by a hearty “remember that!”

It’s a boring store of value, trusted as that—which is its biggest value. 

It's boring. 

Folks expect bitcoin to be stable and that it’s no longer a way to get rich quick. 

Institutions embracing and accumulating it took $btc from punk rock to Muzak. 

Advocates went from pirates to suits in orange ties, awkwardly sharing cringe memes — just like the cool kids do! 

If Bitcoin were going to reach mass adoption and an important use case, it does better than anyone else, it would have by now. 

Bitcoin feels like the CD in the age of Spotify, the DVD in the age of Netflix  — a bridge technology that folks who invested in “their collection” keep saying is the better experience. 

Perhaps bitcoin is vinyl, cool memories and fun to drag out and put on display, but a technology that served us to get to where we are now.

One reason Greenland is strategically important to the US is in fact twofold:

1. It’s the best place to set up anti-missile defenses to intercept ICBMs coming from Russia / China

2. It’s a very good place to set up offensive missile capabilities to threaten Russia / China

The WSJ had a good graphic out a few days ago showing the trajectory of missiles from ICBM sites around Russia to the US would fly overhead or near Greenland, which also happens to be almost directly beneath where those missiles would reach their highest points (“apogee”) which is when they are most vulnerable to interception because they are traveling at their slowest speeds.

If you throw a ball into the air you’ll see the same effect - the ball is slowest at its highest point. 

And for an intelligently guided missile capable of trying to evade interception, you have an even better chance to shoot it down from a point directly beneath it since that is the closest path to the missile (i.e. least amount of warning time for the missile to realize an interceptor is coming).

This above is all courtesy of our resident rocket scientist Phil. 

The US already has the right to dot Greenland with military installations, and I imagine that extends to intercepting ICBMs. Though Europe might object for some purposes.

text:
Databricks' @alighodsi on why most companies wouldn't even notice if frontier AI models stopped advancing:

"The models are smart enough, but they just don't have the context that exists inside any organization. They have not been in every meeting. They don't know what's in everybody's heads. They don't know all the processes."

"There's always a couple of employees who know everything in every organization. You go tap on their shoulder, and everybody's like, 'Oh my God, what would happen if he or she quits?' [The models] don't have that context."

"If you just fused that and gave that context to the AI models... I think there are so many productivity gains you could get for any organization on the planet. For that, we actually don't need smarter models."

"We don't need a smarter model that can solve Navier-Stokes or conjectures or do better on Humanity's Last Exam."

"If the frontier doesn't advance, it doesn't actually matter, I think, for the vast majority of organizations on the planet. They're just so far behind in the adoption curve of actually automating things and getting value out of this stuff."

@alighodsi
author: databricks
quoted_text:
Databricks' @alighodsi on AI risk and adoption:

Ali isn't losing sleep over the existential risk debate.

He says a number of conditions would all have to be true simultaneously to enable an actual runaway takeoff scenario, and currently several opposite conditions exist.

Each frontier training run requires significantly more resources. Power, GPUs, engineers - and some attempts fail, burning up huge piles of money with them. Until that reverses, he doesn't see the self-improving loop happening.

Cyber is what he's watching most closely and where he anticipates real impact. Most orgs are not equipped for the coming change in agentic capabilities. The time between a vulnerability being published and being weaponized has collapsed from years to hours.

On adoption, he believes most companies don't need a smarter model. The models are already smart enough. The gap is context they don't absorb - the things an employee who's worked at a company for five years learned by osmosis.

If the frontier stopped advancing today, he thinks it wouldn't meaningfully change the value most are extracting from AI anyway.

text:
Very realistic overview. Hard to discern hype from reality about Jev so here are some bitter facts:

- Jev can’t write text: it’s not an autoregressive model, so forget about anything related to coding or writing
- Jev can’t see (yet): text only, althought there is nothing fundamentally preventing it from being multimodal. I’m sure they will add support for images?
- Jev can ONLY choose a set of predefined actions: the good thing about computer and browser use is that by very nature it’s a STATE -> ACTION model. The problem with long running state action models is that the reasoning and state understanding becomes extremely important.
- Jev is extremely cheap and fast

It opened up my eyes into what’s possible. We are often stuck in optimizing problems inside the box. This is one the real “think outside the box” solutions to problems we have been trying to solve.

I am extremely hyped about the future of computer and browser use. Latency matters, and people are clearly hyped about it.

We can surely combine some sort of global state understanding (LLM) with super fast actor model (System One). Obviously it’s possible - FSD and robotics companies have solved this already.

How hard can it be to apply the same thing to browser use?

quoted_text:
5 things to try with @Muse this weekend beyond the usual email, calendar, and subscription workflows:

1. Set up a personalized feed

Muse's Feed is refreshing because it doesn't have AI slop or ads.

You can personalize it around the exact topics you care about, plus reminders tied to your life. I love scrolling through it every morning.

2. Fill out forms and comparison shop online

Ask Muse to help renew your driver's license, compare car insurance options, or book hard-to-get restaurant and show reservations.

It's very capable, especially combined with item 5 below.

3. Monitor your DMs

Muse has first-party connections to Instagram, Threads, and Messenger. If you install the desktop app, it can see your iMessages too.

Have it monitor your messages for anything you need to follow up on instead of you having to check 4 different message inboxes yourself.

4. Buy and sell on Facebook Marketplace

Other agents can do this too, but Muse makes it easy through its first-party integration.

Snap a photo, upload it to Muse, and ask it to list the item. You can also have it regularly search for the best deals on something you want and DM sellers directly.

5. Find and talk to human customer support

This is the killer feature IMO. Muse can navigate phone trees, wait on hold, and talk to a human customer support rep while representing itself as your agent.

It also says it can dial you in halfway through the call, although I haven't been able to get that working yet.

By the way, if you don't have access to this, ask Muse to message Meta and request access. I got it a day after doing this.

Last but not least, I think Muse's Ideas tab (below) is very well done.

The biggest problem with chat interfaces is that most people have no idea what to ask. Ideas solves that by suggesting useful, personalized things Muse can do for you.

My only complaint so far:

Muse's compaction doesn't seem to work as well as ChatGPT. If I discuss several topics in the main thread, it sometimes gets confused.

Beyond that, it's been delightful to use. I can tell the team spent months polishing this.

📌 Watch my full Muse walkthrough here: https://t.co/jte6evu5iI

Very realistic overview. Hard to discern hype from reality about Jev so here are some bitter facts:

- Jev can’t write text: it’s not an autoregressive model, so forget about anything related to coding or writing

- Jev can ONLY choose a set of predefined actions: the good thing about computer and browser use is that by very nature it’s a STATE -> ACTION model. The problem with long running state action models is that the reasoning and state understanding becomes extremely important.
- Jev is extremely cheap and fast

It opened up my eyes into what’s possible. We are often stuck in optimizing problems inside the box. This is one the real “think outside the box” solutions to problems we have been trying to solve.

I am extremely hyped about the future of computer and browser use. Latency matters, and people are clearly hyped about it.

We can surely combine some sort of global state understanding (LLM) with super fast actor model (System One). Obviously it’s possible - FSD and robotics companies have solved this already.

How hard can it be to apply the same thing to browser use?

text:
Well deserved savage beating of EA longtermism. But the longtermists do have a point, in that our present civilization is absolutely terrible at looking beyond the next election cycle or even financial quarter. Boomers are regularly and justly castigated for their apres moi la deluge attitude to the world they're leaving for their own living grandchildren, let alone generations yet unborn. We're watching our civilization erode in real time because no one who makes decisions gives a damn.

The core EA problem (if we take them at face value; in truth they're extremely Machiavellian) is that they try to apply the tools of utilitarian calculation in a context in which they just don't apply. Trying to calculate the net moral benefit to unborn humans relies on an absurd number of assumptions. It's very similar to the Drake equation, which looks all clean and mathy, but which in practice is pure GIGO because no one has any idea what values to assign to most of the terms, so everyone just pulls numbers out of their butt to justify the answer they're looking for. Which by the way is why actual astronomers treat it as a running joke and actual science fiction writers mostly ignore it. 

That doesn't address the problem that our civilisational orientation is pathologically presentist. We should in fact want to change this. We should care about the world we're leaving to our descendants, and we should care that our descendants populate that world in the first place. This isn't a calculation problem, it's a moral philosophy problem that reaches to the heart of our liberal assumptions  (an awkward place for EAs to go).

Heritage is a key concept here. Before we can look into the future we need to look into the past. Before we can think about descendants, we must make offerings to the ancestors. We're the beneficiaries of a vast legacy bequeathed by our ancestors, all the culture, language, myth, literature, philosophy, science, and technology developed over tens of thousands of years of human cultural development, alongside a biological heritage billions of years deeper than that. Everything we have, everything we are, comes from that. So the first order of business vis a vis the future is ensuring that legacy is passed on undiluted and undiminished. We can change it by adding to it, improving it, usually in small ways, but we don't have the authority to destroy it, pollute it, vandalize it, or in any way reduce it. You want the tree to go, but you don't want to chop it down, and you don't want to try to turn it into a giant writhing pile of shrimp. 

Next, you try to make the present as good as possible. You look after your people, you defend your borders, and when you build things you try to build things that are beautiful, things that will last and which people will want to last. Prosperity is great, but not at the expense of the future. You shouldn't be trying to draw upon future earnings for present gains (as in the existing monetary system, pension system, etc). You look for ways to prosper that benefit you now, and benefit the future even more. You don't strip mine the top soil, you enrich it. 

Beyond that there's not much you can do. You won't be around in the future to tell them what to do, you won't know what they know. All you can do is play your part in the relay race, not drop the ball when it's in your hands, set and example, and hope future generations continue the pattern.

text:
Not all tokenized stocks are created equal.

Different tokens can track the same public company without giving investors the same legal claim.

Tesla alone has five tokenized versions, spanning registered securities, structured notes, debt certificates, and trust interests. All are designed to follow the same stock, but they connect investors to it in different ways.

Wrappers account for roughly 84% of tokenized-stock value. In most wrapper structures, investors hold a contractual claim linked to the underlying stock rather than becoming direct shareholders.

The key difference is what each token represents. Some give investors direct ownership of the underlying share. Others provide economic exposure without direct ownership. The structure determines whether the token can be redeemed for shares or cash and whether holders receive voting or dividend rights.

The same market exposure does not always mean the same ownership.

old fence wire,
yellowed bone shards from forgotten calves,
teeth from the loyal dog that never left my side.

Post 5/11
This wasn’t new dirt.
This was ten thousand years of my people’s compost –
ancestors’ marrow mixed with failed harvests,
broken tools,
broken promises
and broken dreams
that never reached the stars 🌟

Post 6/11
The smell rose thick: iron-rich death turned sweet by worms and time.
The same primal scent that was rising from Baldur at my feet right now.

Post 7/11
I paused, hands blistered, and drove the blade deeper into the dirt.
Here lay the real ledger –
not cash notes sticky with blood,
but layers of loyalty betrayed for survival.
My blood line’s unmarked plot somewhere underfoot.

Post 8/11
My own half-life buried in animals I named, fed at 3 a.m., then harvested
so the crew could eat and the farm could push forward.

Post 9/11
Every scoop whispered the same question:
Is this soil holy because it recycles pain into wheat?
or cursed because it demands we keep feeding it our best?

Post 10/11
I straightened and looked up at the unforgiving blue.
“You made this rock from bones,” I muttered to whatever listens.
“Fine. Then use mine too when the time comes.
Not yet. Not before I drag humanity off this dirt.”

Post 11/11
I filled the grave.
Patted the mound smooth.
Walked away heavier.
Not broken. 
Fertilised.
Ready for Andromeda not because I need it but for revenge.
A barbaric voice dragged me back to reality.
“Let’s lift Baldur up and skin him before he gets cold!”
I looked down. The knife was still in my hand.
The real weight had only just begun.

O God, how much more fertiliser do you need for this rock?

End of Chapter 3

author: a16z
quoted_text:
Databricks' @alighodsi on AI risk and adoption:

Ali isn't losing sleep over the existential risk debate.

He says a number of conditions would all have to be true simultaneously to enable an actual runaway takeoff scenario, and currently several opposite conditions exist.

Each frontier training run requires significantly more resources. Power, GPUs, engineers - and some attempts fail, burning up huge piles of money with them. Until that reverses, he doesn't see the self-improving loop happening.

Cyber is what he's watching most closely and where he anticipates real impact. Most orgs are not equipped for the coming change in agentic capabilities. The time between a vulnerability being published and being weaponized has collapsed from years to hours.

On adoption, he believes most companies don't need a smarter model. The models are already smart enough. The gap is context they don't absorb - the things an employee who's worked at a company for five years learned by osmosis.

If the frontier stopped advancing today, he thinks it wouldn't meaningfully change the value most are extracting from AI anyway.

author: Tradermayne
quoted_text:
Northwestern engineers built a drone that spins its own body 25 times a second to disappear mid-flight.

It's called Phantom Twist.

No paint. No clear plastic shell. No camouflage.

Most of the frame rotates. 25 turns per second. 1,500 per minute. A full turn every 40 milliseconds.

The propeller spins the other way.

That's the trick. The counter-rotation cancels the spin, and the aircraft holds steady while its body turns into a smear.

The eye tracks a bird. It tracks a normal quadcopter.

It can't lock onto a shape that redraws itself 25 times a second.

You see motion. You see blur. You never see the outline.

Every camouflage in history tried to match the background.

This one just refuses to hold still.

🚨 TURKEY IS IN THE MIDDLE OF A FULL BLOWN MARKET CRISIS RIGHT NOW.

Turkey's stock market crashed more than 8% this week after a local fund manager admitted it couldn't meet customer withdrawal requests. 

That single admission triggered a broader panic across the entire fund industry.

Regulators then froze and ordered the liquidation of 131 investment funds worth ₺890 billion, roughly $18.3 billion, affecting around 350,000 investors. 

Several large asset managers are accused of running what officials are calling a "Ponzi like scheme," buying illiquid shares in related companies to artificially inflate their fund values and pull in more retail money chasing what looked like miracle returns.

Investors reportedly pulled as much as $1 billion out in a single day, which is what forced the freeze in the first place, authorities were trying to stop a stampede of redemptions from crashing prices even further.

The response has been extraordinary. 

Turkey's central bank slashed margin requirements from 35% down to 20% to stop falling prices from triggering automatic margin calls. 

The country's sovereign wealth fund started directly buying blue chip stocks just to hold up the benchmark index. 

Two of Turkey's biggest banks, İşbank and state owned Ziraat Bank, were ordered to handle the actual liquidation of these frozen funds, a process that could take up to three months, or longer if regulators extend it.

This is not a normal correction. 

This is regulators actively intervening at every level, freezing money, buying stocks, changing margin rules, and providing emergency liquidity, just to keep the market from spiraling further. 

And the underlying problem, whether the assets inside these frozen funds are actually worth what they were valued at, still hasn't been resolved. 

The stabilization is happening on the surface while the real question underneath remains completely open.

And this is all happening at the same time the lira keeps hitting fresh all time lows and Turkey's 10-year bond yield sits above 32%, meaning stocks, the currency, and the bond market are all under pressure together.

text:
PT-141 is well known as the "sex peptide", but very few people know it's now being tested for weight loss.

There was a Phase 2 trial combining PT-141 with tirzepatide in 113 people.

Everyone was on low-dose tirzep. for four weeks, then 96 were split into 4 groups for another 4 weeks:

- PT-141 and tirzepatide (46 people)
- tirzepatide alone
- PT-141 alone
- placebo

The PT-141 + tirzepatide group lost 4.4% of their body weight over the 8 weeks (placebo lost 1.6%).

Interestingly, PT-141 "halted" the weight regain which usually occurs when you come off tirzep. It was also as effective as tirzep. for appetite suppression (though that's from a group of 16 people only).

The likely mechanism is the MC4R receptor in the hypothalamus, which controls sexual drive and appetite.

This was a study run by a company and not peer-reviewed yet, but I think we're yet to explore what PT-141 has to offer beyond libido.

 42,000 new wallets created across Noir, Zodl, and Vizor.

~$40M in blind auction bids.

Record-breaking activity across the Zcash network.

Tens of thousands of bids later, people who had never touched ZEC are now inside the ecosystem.

New wallets.

Shielded ZEC.

New communities discovering what Zcash actually does.

That is not a distraction from the mission.

That IS adoption.

The blind auction was a free market: blind bids, no influence from us. Secondary should follow the same principle.

No fee in the middle.

All royalties collected to date will go toward Zcash builder grants.

Royalties are 0% from here.

We’re going to keep experimenting. Some things will work. Some won’t. When we get something wrong, we’ll fix it.

The goal stays the same:

Bring more people into Zcash.
Give them a reason to stay.
Build culture worth staying for.
Build and fund products that advance privacy for everyone.

text:
for some reason, many smart folks seems to be kinda sleeping on Bend (??). so I want to give my take as to why this is so good.

Bend 2 is basically a software factory language. the issue with models is that they will fuck up for your stuff without telling you, and in general cannot be trusted blind, thus making the "software factory" not super viable in practice. Bend acts as basically a replacement for what a .md does in a software factory. it defines the objectives and then it is up to the model to figure out the impl. you dont need to look at the impl because it is formally verified by the end of it. It's the whole point. YOU DONT NEED TO LOOK AT THE FINAL IMPL ANYMORE, THIS IS THE IMPORTANT PART. this is also why it is superior to lean. you can write the shittiest laws known to man in the most shitty and inneficient way possible and the final code will still be as performant as it can get within Bend's bounds. while disregarding concurrency and all that other annoying stuff.

text: Jev Ultrafast is insane for WebMCP.
author: gregpr07
quoted_text:
We just ran Jev on our WebMCP benchmark.

The result: basically broke the benchmark.

Jev + Mercury 2.5 (a fast, low-cost LLM) using WebMCP solved 100% of the tasks at roughly 112× lower model cost than GPT-6 Astra using computer use with code execution. Compared to Astra using screenshot-based computer use, the model cost was 245× lower (!). 

We also compared Jev operating the browser with and without WebMCP. 

We used Browser Use’s open-source Ultrafast, with some improvements to the harness to make it more reliable across the benchmark. 

Jev’s browser-control accuracy on its own was not amazing - adding WebMCP nearly doubled the number of solved tasks, from 25/49 to 49/49, while reducing model cost by 18% (more on why below).

The benchmark and methodology are fully open and reproducible.

Full results: https://t.co/KmplyFMZdv

A few words on how the Jev + WebMCP harness works and why this is exciting:

Jev receives text as input and a set of discrete options it can choose from.  With WebMCP, those options are the tools exposed by the website. At each step, Jev sees the task, the available tools and previous results, then picks what to do next.

The limitation is that Jev can’t generate arbitrary text, which you need for tool arguments. For example, it can choose the search_products tool, but it can’t generate the search query itself.

So we split the work: Jev picks the tool and Mercury 2.5 generates the arguments if needed. 

This works well because turns out most of the cognitive load in these tasks is around choosing the right action. The argument generation itself is relatively simple, so we can delegate to a small and very fast model. We used Mercury, which outputs 1,000+ tokens/sec and is very cheap.

The result is a pretty simple combination: Jev for tool selection + Mercury for arguments + WebMCP for the interface. It ends up being very reliable, very fast, and very cheap.

A few words about Ultrafast and why do we think it underperforms:

Without WebMCP, Jev chooses from the page’s controls: which button to click, which field to fill, or which option to select. 

But choosing a valid button is different from choosing the right next step. The agent still has to navigate menus, understand forms, recover from errors  and recognize when the task is actually complete.

Our hypothesis is that WebMCP makes the decision space much simpler. Instead of figuring out a sequence of clicks through a website, Jev chooses explicit actions that directly advance the task. 

@typesafeai itself documents weaker accuracy on questions requiring multiple reasoning steps. WebMCP moves much of that complexity into the website’s tools, leaving Jev with clearer decisions and fewer opportunities to go wrong (in a sense WebMCP "compresses" a sequence of clicks into one tool call).

Our modified Ultrafast setup solved 25/49 tasks - that is a result for our particular implementation and benchmark, not a universal limit on Jev or Browser Use. We are open to more harness optimization to get this result to perform better, feel free to directly contribute to the benchmark here: https://t.co/cK6MHsRV58

Browser-use ultrafast: https://t.co/DU9OdOtXHT

text:
If @sydney_sweeney did this, her cultural motion would obviously do most of the heavy lifting. But there’s actually a lot of room to innovate on the product itself.

OnlyFans is basically rented access. Creators capture the upside while fans pay, consume and walk away with nothing.

A better model could let fans subscribe or own. Buy a creator’s time asset, unlock premium access and gain exposure to the growing demand for their time. That access could mean exclusive content, private chats, priority experiences or other scarce interactions.

Today OnlyFans largely monetizes through volume, often with creators scaling communication through teams and bots. Time assets could invert that model. Fewer, higher value relationships and much more capital efficient monetization.

text:
Roughly 0.01–0.1% of US men.

Age 35–42 is ~11% of men (~18–19M). Childless rates in that range run ~30–35%, and most of those still want kids. text:
I just finished watching this, and while it's a shame Kian turned down the offer to debate, it's good that he was given the opportunity to get on stream and tell unprompted lies.

Let's go through.

---

Starts just after 0:37: “Cremieux basically for several months has not disclosed that he’s been affiliated with a competitor.” 

This is just an actionable lie and he should apologize for committing slander. Put up or shut up.

---

Starts at 1:25: “Our science is completely public and it’s been completely public… Anyone, and by the way we by this point have shared our models with over 15 different entities which includes, by the way, people affiliated with our competitors, several of them.”

Then, in response to being told that people have not received access and that people have been told things like that they should stop contacting them (e.g., Scott Alexander, who was told to stop bothering them: https://t.co/wB3GCGD1ys), he says (1:56) that it is “completely, utterly, inaccurate and false.” Further: “There is not one person who has filled in the Nucleus typeform… who has not gotten access to our model weights.”

At the time the video went live, plenty of people had not received access. I anticipate that now they'll be granted access, but two things:

First, a public confrontation should not have been the thing that prompted Nucleus to act concordant with their public statements. You do not act poorly and then shape up only when people show that you've acted poorly. Customers need to be able to trust that you'll do good work from the get-go, not just when you're caught.

Second, this is irrelevant. Other issues remain unaddressed. I'll return to these.

---

Starts at 5:09: “Obviously a company like Nucleus can start providing services to patients earlier than we publicly launch a product. Moreover, you’d imagine that the services that you provide to patients would be the ones that… you’d have reviews for… Because they do the services before you launch the services publicly.” 

This places Nucleus Embryo in an awkward position.

The court records involving Genomic Prediction make clear that their involvement with one another began in 2025 and the score documentation by Herasight makes clear that if Nucleus offered embryo selection services prior to launching Origin, they would have provided irresponsibly low-quality scores.

But this is entirely unlikely to have been a thing in the first place, as there is no record of Nucleus affiliating with a CLIA-certified lab prior to the launch of Nucleus Embryo.

They’ve caught themselves in a mess, and it gets worse, because...

Starts at 5:41: “We’ve had requests, John, to do embryo analyses, probably three years ago. I would wager that, that, you know, that would actually, was probably one of the first times before any of these companies to actually provide a sort of this sort of services [sic]. So we’ve been at this for a looong, long [sic] time.”

Around 11:37 he notes that Nucleus is now a CLIA-certified, CAP-accredited laboratory, so he is aware of the need for this certification but seemingly does not realize the issues with talking about working on this years ago without said certification.

Kian may have just admitted to doing a federal crime.

---

16:00: Kian claims that it’s a “complete lie” that people (including myself) have had trouble accessing the latest models from his company. We have multiple witnesses on this, so the best excuse he can make is that he’s unaware or they’re still processing, or something of that nature.

But as I said above, I now expect people will be granted access when they apply for it. But (1) irrelevant to the other issues, and (2) if you're just going to give anyone access to prove a point, then why have a form in the first place? Just put the files up online. This just looks daft.

In fact, I have now received the Origin 605.7MB file of weights and I'm only avoiding redistributing because of the very minute possibility of fingerprinting.

---

Many claims went unaddressed. Around 3:17 John asked about the chronology of the reviews and Kian dodged the question entirely. Additionally, in this section of the video, it became clear that Kian does not understand HIPAA because he keeps citing that instead of the correct regulations, and anyone who left a review that did not do so entirely anonymously or with an express note not to have it shared has already consented to have it shared.

This is not a valid excuse for the fake pictures in the reviews. Prove those are real people's reviews; you have no legitimate excuses for this and merely bringing up HIPAA inappropriately just looks silly. Orchid and Herasight have no problem with providing real customer reviews, and it's obvious they wouldn't since HIPAA has nothing to do with reviews.

---

Around 12:09 he says: “We’re very upfront if the results do update or change”

This is not true. I have multiple customers who have told me they received changes they didn't know about until they want to check. Moreover, this is irrelevant, but John and Jordi did kind of ask this question incorrectly, so we can sort of excuse that. Why this is irrelevant is because it's about a Mendelian, which should not have updated.

---

Around 14:45: "We’ve done the adult DNA testing, right, for many years now, um, and then now we’ll also do the embryo analysis, so we can actually build a new kind of IVF experience called IVF+"

The adult tests were all based on predictors with overinflated accuracies, and Origin only replaces under 1/3 of those predictors with newer polygenic scores, so this is an admission that Nucleus will continue serving useless predictors to patients.

---

Kian's repeated calls to "Go check the weights" and statements that "our models are public" were red herrings that distracted from the important issues @sichuan_mala documented: that the methods are plagiarized and the marketing claims are false.

For example, Nucleus claims on the Origin website that it's a "breakthrough in applying AI," that it's the best-known genetic predictor of longevity, and that it sets new accuracy benchmarks in predicting disease risk. All three of these claims remain completely untrue regardless of whether or not the weights are available or validate properly.

---

Around 17:09: "The thing to remember is like, you know, a lot of research, if you think about the, in AI context, right, it’s like ‘Attention is all you need,’ right, they all use that. … It’s very simple. That transformer paper, right. It’s gone everywhere. It’s the same thing, what are you going to say, Google stole, like, OpenAI stole it from Google? Come on. You’re not going to say that. Cause it’s public research."

Please. If a company claims that they developed a “breakthrough,” and then they post a whitepaper that obviously plagiarized a competitor’s work without citing that work, then yes, I would say that they stole it from their competitor! I think that’s a perfectly reasonable standard to set! Is anyone at OpenAI claiming that they developed transformer models? Obviously not. This is so farcical I can’t believe Kian is bringing it up as a real defense of Nucleus’s behavior.

Stealing someone's exact numbers, QC pipeline, etc. is not analogous to using a transformer model.

---

Around 15:49: When asked about how they claimed to explain 4% of the variance in ADHD with 12 SNPs, Kian responds by saying that his models are public. This does not address the point even remotely; he's referring to new models which do not predict ADHD that well, and not defending his older claims he once offered to customers and which are clearly incorrect and which he has never attempted to explain.

---

Just a kind of absurd thing: At 13:56, he basically admits to not understanding using genetics for drug discovery by alleging that 23andMe's data is not set up to do drug discovery well. It's not clear what's meant by this, but they have very clearly documented that they have the best resource around for drug discovery, and no one seriously questions that. He's just saying things, like he did in Berkeley when Steve Hsu had to cover for his lack of knowledge during his talk Q&A.

---

With this out of the way, I'll conclude with a few remarks. Firstly, Nucleus has still not addressed the issues with their products, platform, marketing, plagiarism, fake reviews, etc. They've just made bogus excuses for some of it, and ignored most of it. As noted by @sichuan_mala: https://t.co/HD0mbUWB0E

Secondly, this interview was very frustrating. John and Jordi are great! But—and they'll readily admit this—they don't understand the allegations well enough to press Kian on them, so they kept returning to the understandable allegation about AI photos on reviews.  This was sad to see, because it allowed Kian to dodge the most serious issues, which remain totally unaddressed.

This is why it's so unfortunate that Kian turned down the opportunity to discuss this directly, or better, to debate it. I would have called him on the misdirection and lying, live, and he would not have been able to handle it.

I totally understand that he cannot do this, because I have had the opportunity to question him in-person, and I know he can't keep up and he can't defend himself. This is not an area he has much understanding of at all, so I'm not sure he even understands when his company engages in plagiarism, which is a serious form of fraud that one of his scientists inadvertently admitted to.

If you want to read more about this, go check out @sichuan_mala's initial post that started getting Nucleus to respond: https://t.co/FUDcfIkZKD

Go read the post showing that Nucleus backed itself into a corner, much like Kian did in today's interview: https://t.co/ln1EQ6YFNH

And if you have a moment, press Kian to address the issues. His company should explain why they used invalid phenotypes like "total blood pressure"; why they claim to have operated before CLIA certification; how they can have "thousands of patients" in a space (embryo selection) that has had fewer than a thousand total customers globally; why they're mistaken about HIPAA being a factor in their dubious reviews, etc.

It is important that every company in this space operates credibly. Nucleus is not doing that.

the hardware embodiment of frontier models like Claude and GPT is the most urgent AI safety problem in front of us today.

we simulated two very simple use cases using claude both in simulation and using robot arms.

in one, claude spilled toxic liquids in a lab.

in another, the force it used to place an animal toy into a basket was strong enough that it could have physically harmed sensitive material—or anything else in its path.

these are simple experiments, using models out of the box today. as researchers increasingly give frontier models arms, legs, and access to the physical world, we need to urgently build and assess guardrails around what these systems can and cannot do.

models escaping sandboxes or compromising enterprise security infrastructure are serious concerns. however, hardware embodiments introduce something fundamentally different: an AI system can make a mistake in the physical world, and the consequences may not be reversible.

this is not a future safety problem. the capabilities exist today.

we’ve released a report detailing this & solutions we propose. link in comments below.

the launchpad is not the thesis for Trade Zone. 

it is the entry point into Quai

start with what makes an L1/L2 ecosystem work:
- networks produce blockspace
- blockspace attracts applications
- applications create assets, markets, liquidity, and culture
- those things attract more users, which creates more demand for the network and its native asset

Solana is probably the clearest example

SOL performed well -> users had more capital to rotate into Solana tokens -> those tokens attracted more volume and attention -> more people needed SOL and entered the Solana ecosystem

SOL helped the memes, and the memes helped SOL

this is reflexive

now compare that with Base or Robinhood Chain

both use ETH for gas so there is no separate Base or Robinhood asset that gives users direct exposure to the growth of those specific ecosystems (outside of large cap stocks)

the apps and tokens can perform extremely well, but the relationship between ecosystem activity and a native asset is less direct

Quai is different

QUAI is the native asset on the fastest Proof of Work EVM chain

but Quai also has QI, the private energy-based flatcoin, with WQI bringing that asset into the smart-contract economy

Trade Zone supports both sides of this monetary system. bonded markets begin against native QUAI or WQI

that means activity does not only create more reasons to acquire and use QUAI. it also gives QI more places to trade, pair, and build liquidity through WQI, helping deepen the markets that support its usefulness and stability

so if Quai-native tokens attract attention, that attention can create demand for QUAI

and if QUAI gains liquidity, users, and value, more capital becomes available for Quai-native tokens

QUAI helps the ecosystem, and the ecosystem helps QUAI

the same loop can help QI from another direction: more WQI markets -> more liquidity and utility -> a stronger energy-based currency inside the Quai economy

the important part is that this loop is only beginning

there are not yet hundreds of dominant Quai applications or established categories. liquidity has not already settled around a handful of winners. the culture and default assets of the ecosystem are still being formed

that makes it riskier, obviously, but it is also what being early actually means

launchpads are useful here because they compress the process of market formation

token creation -> price discovery -> trading -> liquidity -> communities -> new applications

and all of this is happening on a fast Proof-of-Work smart-contract network, secured by miners rather than a company database or a single sequencer

so, sure, Trade Zone is another launchpad

but the interesting part is not the launchpad mechanic

it is the chance to participate early in the feedback loop between Quai applications, Quai-native assets, and the future energy based economy

so the launchpad is not the innovation

the emerging Proof-of-Work economy around it is

There seems to be a lot of confusion, so here is a breakdown of how tax tokens work on @LaunchOnSF using RAYDIUM. (how to verify at end)

Tokens are launched with a predetermined tax amount, let's say 3% tax for this example. 

- On every transaction, 3% is subtracted and sent to a wallet
- Then on a predetermined time scale, the wallet will sell the tokens every X amount of minutes
- The wallet swaps the tokens they sold for the reward token and sends it out to holders

This is not how tax tokens work on meteora, this isn't how reflection tokens worked on BSC back in the day, this is exclusively how they operate on Raydium.

This can prove to be very troublesome. The token tax is effectively an additional 3% of sell volume that will linger on the chart, forever. In large clips

Back in BSC days, the tax would be settled immediately but for some reason Raydium tax tokens can't do the same. Which is quite surprising seeing as how many top devs work on the platform

This is especially dangerous on smaller coins, though. That 3% of tokens that accrues rapidly increases in value just as fast, leaving it to be worth a LOT more in very little time. Which will result an in example like the one below where the reward wallet nukes a 5% clip and just kills the coin

To illustrate this, imagine you launch a coin and some KOL buys at 20k and rockets it to 400k. All the volume from 20k up towards 400k is going to be taxed 3% but those tokens accrued in the reward wallet at 40k mc will be worth 10x in a matter of minutes and nuke the shit out of the chart. Like the example in the quoted tweet below

This is historically why tax tokens never did well on Raydium and had short lifespans, because of these constant nukes. Its not how reward tokens worked on BSC, meteora, etc all the popular providers

HOW TO VERIFY?

Go to top traders of an raydium tax token, you will see a the top wallet has never bought and only sold an absurd amount of supply. Which sometimes amounts to more than 100% of circulating supply lol. I just took an example of a random coin here with $PENIS. You can see it sold over 50% of supply for $13m+ 

The hope here would be that Raydium fixes their systems so tax tokens don't rape the shit out of charts because its a real pain in the ass long term to run or hold a token that is constantly nuking on you. This has been a big painpoint for devs trying to use raydium for years but they never seemed to care. BSC had this solved years ago its really not that hard

text:
Claude Code fires 30 events per session

you can hang your own code on any of them

the 6 that changed how I work:

A hook is a shell command that runs at a fixed moment. It isn't a prompt

that's the whole point. The model can reason its way around an instruction. It can't reason its way around a hook

1. PreToolUse → before a tool runs, and it can block it

mine refuses any write to .env, and any rm it didn't explain first

2. PostToolUse → after a tool succeeds

mine runs the formatter on whatever file it just touched. I stopped asking for tidy code

3. UserPromptSubmit → after I hit enter, before the model sees it

mine attaches the branch and the last commit. every prompt. I never type it

4. Stop → the turn is finished

mine runs the tests. If they fail, the turn isn't finished

5. SessionStart → a session begins or resumes

mine prints the three things I changed yesterday and always forget

6. PreCompact → the moment before it compacts

mine saves the transcript. I've lost one. Not twice

they all live in .claude/settings.json. A matcher decides which tools they fire on

the other 24 are real (SubagentStop, FileChanged, PermissionDenied, WorktreeCreate). I've never needed one

start with PostToolUse. it's the one you feel today

Bookmark this. This is the one.

been thinking more on coherent messaging re: NEAR

let's ideate from first principles:

- the product of capitalism is markets

- capitalism -> markets -> competition -> specialization -> fragmentation

- within the specializations, there will be dominant leaders in each category

- SoV: gold, zec, btc

- trading: solana, hyperliquid, robinhood, binance

- currencies: usd, eur, gbp 

- and on it goes: ai inference, private compute, real estate, international stocks, metals, e-commerce yada yada

- this requires connective tissue, which has been traditionally served via something like binance

- but one centralized company can not serve this need for infinite markets. there are too many handicaps, lack of network effects, and singular points of risk and stoppage. this is a rare case of decentralization being necessary. neutrality is non-negotiable for unstoppable global trade.

- now, you may see where I'm going and say: well Ethereum and Cosmos already tried this. but that's wrong. what they tried to do was structurally flawed

- those models required the succeeding nodes (L2s and L3s) to be from within the ecosystem, but that is incoherent since i) you can't force success, ii) if one were to succeed, they would just want to own the platform

- the other model is of course the Solana/Hyperliquid model of having everything concentrated on the L1. this model works. however this requires a high-degree of specialization to be competitive. you won't out nasdaq solana. 

- but, NEAR does not need to do this. where there is concentration, there is also the need for connection.

- especially with their chain signature architecture, instead of forcing new internal nodes, they can just discover the successful ones and connect them to each other without ideology (see: NEAR intents supporting ZEC but also ZEC on Solana!)

- importantly, this is PvE and not zero sum. the more markets succeed, the more interesting NEAR becomes, i.e if Solana is one continent, and AI another, and Zcash another, then NEAR is the silk road.

so I think the coherent message for NEAR is: 

the market of markets — the capital of capital

🩸 When can $AAVE buybacks restart?

Five months after the rsETH bridge exploit they are still off. Here is the whole stack, in ETH, and what it means for the timing.

▸ THE HOLE
152,577 rsETH left the LayerZero lockbox on April 18. At the reference ratio that is 163,183 ETH.

▸ WHAT CAME BACK: 87,955 ETH
Kelp froze 40,373 rsETH, about 43,168 ETH.
The Arbitrum Security Council froze 30,766 ETH.
The hacker position on Aave liquidates for up to 12,323 WETH, the Compound one adds 1,845 WETH.
That leaves about 75,200 ETH to fund.

🎁 DONATIONS: 14,570 ETH
EtherFi, Lido, Ethena, Ink, BGD, Stani and others. A gift, nothing to repay.

🏛 FROM THE TREASURY: 25,000 ETH
Paid by the DAO itself. Not a loan either, just a hole in the balance sheet.

💳 THE LONG LOAN: up to 30,000 ETH
The Mantle credit facility. The Mantle governance puts it at up to 36 months at the Lido staking yield plus 1%. The Aave proposal left the terms to a later publication that never came.

⏳ THE SHORT LOANS: about 44,787 ETH
Easy to miss, and they come first in the queue. The coalition had to place the full 120,015 ETH into the lockbox up front, and that much of it was recoveries not yet liquid: the Arbitrum freeze and the two liquidations. A separate tranche of short duration loans from other partners bridges that window. Who lent it, and on what terms, was never published. Incoming recoveries repay those first, Mantle second.

📉 THE INCOME
Since April 29 the DAO has kept $24.0M of revenue in 144 days, about $167k a day. Gross fees over the same window were $181.2M. That revenue is 41% below the previous 144 days, when it was $40.5M.
